name: Gajar Halwa
cuisine: North Indian (Punjab and Delhi winter dessert, now pan-Indian)

ingredients.name: Carrot (gajar), red Delhi carrot if available, else orange

equipment: Heavy-bottomed kadai or deep non-stick pan: a heavy base spreads the heat and reduces scorching
Grater (box grater, coarse side): for the carrots
Wooden spoon or flat spatula: for stirring and scraping the base
Small pan or bowl, knife and board: for the nuts and cardamom
Measuring spoons, cup or jug, kitchen scale (or use the household measures)
Pressure cooker (optional): some sources cook the carrots in milk in a cooker for speed; this recipe uses the open pan so you can watch it

steps.title: Wash and peel the carrots
steps.text: Wash 200 g carrots under running water and scrape off the skin with a peeler.
steps.visualCue: The carrots look smooth and evenly orange or red with no brown patches
steps.cameraCheck: The peeled carrots on the board
steps.videoShot: A peeler stripping the skin off one carrot.
steps.watchOut: Leaving dirt in the cracks near the top, which gives a gritty halwa; trim the top 1 cm off and rinse again.

steps.title: Grate the carrots
steps.text: Grate the carrots on the coarse side of the grater into a bowl.
steps.visualCue: A loose pile of orange threads, about 1½ cups packed
steps.videoShot: Carrot strands falling into the bowl from the grater.
steps.watchOut: Grating the last stub so short that your knuckles scrape; stop at about 2 cm and chop the stub finely instead.

steps.title: Prepare the nuts and cardamom
steps.text: Chop 4 cashews into halves or quarters. Open 2 cardamom pods and crush the seeds with the back of a spoon.
steps.visualCue: Small cashew pieces, and a coarse dark cardamom powder that smells sweet and floral
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped cashews and crushed cardamom in a small bowl
steps.videoShot: A knife cutting a cashew, then a spoon crushing the cardamom seeds.
steps.watchOut: Whole cashews that stay hard in the finished halwa; chop them small. A weak cardamom smell means old pods; use 3 pods.

steps.title: Heat the ghee
steps.text: Place the kadai on medium heat and add 1 tbsp (12 g) ghee.
steps.visualCue: The ghee melts fully and spreads into a thin shiny layer with a nutty smell
steps.cameraCheck: The melted ghee in the kadai
steps.videoShot: A spoon of ghee melting in the pan.
steps.watchOut: Smoking ghee, which means the heat is too high and the ghee will taste burnt; lower the flame and let the pan cool a few seconds.

steps.title: Fry the cashews and raisins
steps.text: Add the chopped cashews and stir for 30 seconds, then add 5 g raisins and stir for 10 seconds. Scoop both into a small bowl and keep the ghee in the pan.
steps.visualCue: The cashews turn light golden and the raisins puff up and look plump
steps.cameraCheck: The golden cashews and puffed raisins in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Raisins swelling in ghee, then a spoon lifting them out.
steps.watchOut: Dark brown cashews or black raisins, which taste bitter; take them out the moment the cashews are pale gold, as they keep browning off the heat.

steps.title: Sauté the grated carrot
steps.text: Add all the grated carrot to the same ghee and stir on medium heat.
steps.visualCue: The carrot shrinks a little, turns glossy with ghee and smells sweet and a little roasted
steps.cameraCheck: The glossy carrot in the pan
steps.videoShot: Grated carrot being stirred in ghee until it shines.
steps.watchOut: Browning at the pan edge; if you see brown bits, lower the heat and stir from the bottom. A raw, grassy smell means it needs another minute or two.

steps.title: Add the milk
steps.text: Pour in 150 ml cold milk and stir once.
steps.visualCue: The milk covers the carrot and starts to bubble softly around the edge
steps.videoShot: Milk being poured over the carrot in the kadai.
steps.watchOut: Splitting or curdled milk, which looks like tiny white lumps; use cold milk (source tip) and keep the heat at medium, not high.

steps.title: Simmer on low heat
steps.text: Turn the heat to low-medium and let the carrot and milk simmer, stirring every 1-2 minutes.
steps.visualCue: The milk reduces and thickens, the carrot turns softer and deeper orange, and only a little loose milk is left at the bottom
steps.cameraCheck: The pan showing thickened milk and soft carrot
steps.videoShot: Milk bubbling down around soft carrot threads.
steps.watchOut: Sticking and scorching on the base; if you smell burning, lower the heat and scrape the bottom with the spoon. If the carrot is still hard when the milk is almost gone, add 2 tbsp warm milk and cook 3 min more.

steps.title: Add the sugar
steps.text: Add 25 g (2 tbsp) sugar once the carrot is soft, and stir.
steps.visualCue: The sugar melts into the carrot and the mixture suddenly looks wet and loose again
steps.cameraCheck: The loose, glossy mixture after the sugar melts
steps.videoShot: Sugar crystals dissolving into the carrot.
steps.watchOut: Adding the sugar too early while the carrot is still hard, which keeps the carrot firm; add it after the carrot has softened. The wet look is normal and will cook off.

steps.title: Cook down until dry
steps.text: Keep cooking on medium-low heat, stirring more often, until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan.
steps.visualCue: The halwa looks thick, glossy and fairly dry, clumps together and pulls away from the pan, and ghee shines on the carrot
steps.cameraCheck: The spoon dragged across the pan showing a clear path
steps.videoShot: A spoon dragging a clean line through thick halwa.
steps.watchOut: Taking it off while it is still wet, which gives a watery halwa that goes soggy in the fridge; keep going until you see no liquid when you drag the spoon through it. If it starts to stick, lower the heat.

steps.title: Finish with cardamom and nuts
steps.text: Switch off the heat, stir in the cardamom and the fried cashews and raisins.
steps.visualCue: A sweet, floral cardamom smell rises as you stir, with golden cashews and plump raisins visible through the carrot
steps.cameraCheck: The finished halwa in the pan
steps.videoShot: Nuts and cardamom stirred into the glossy halwa.
steps.watchOut: Adding the cardamom early and cooking it away; add it at the end so the smell stays.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Spoon into a bowl while warm.
steps.tip: Red (Delhi) carrots are sweeter and give a deeper colour; if you only have orange carrots, taste before adding all the sugar.
steps.visualCue: A glossy, deep orange-red mound that holds its shape with ghee at the edges
steps.videoShot: A spoon lifting a shiny scoop of halwa from the bowl.
steps.watchOut: Serving it straight from the hot pan, as the sugar is very hot and can burn your mouth; wait 2 minutes.

reasons: a dessert made from a vegetable, so it brings good fibre (about 6 g), a very large amount of vitamin A from the carrots (about 180% of the day) and some calcium and B12 from milk. Points off for about 25 g of added sugar (100% of the 25 g limit) and about 11 g of saturated fat (about 50% of the limit) from ghee and milk. Restaurant versions often use more sugar, ghee or khoya and bigger bowls (est.).

researchRating.basis: one of India's best-loved winter desserts, published in a very large number of recipe sites, blogs and food-media lists, with the same core recipe across all of them. Points off for the long grating-and-stirring effort and for high sugar and ghee. Recipe-site star counts were not checked this run. Platform dish ratings were not used.

storage: Fridge-safe in a closed container for up to 3 days (est.; cool within 1 hour of cooking). Freezing is possible for about 1 month (est.; not source-checked). Reheat in a pan on low heat with 1-2 tbsp milk, stirring until warm, or microwave in 30 second bursts, stirring in between.
leftoverRemix: Gajar halwa paratha. Spread 2 tbsp leftover halwa inside a small whole-wheat roti, fold, and cook on a tawa with a little ghee until golden on both sides (contains gluten).
burnOff: about 6.1 km of running (430 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 8.6 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 43 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: Not found — vrat vegetable lists differ and no source seen this run says whether carrot is allowed; if allowed, swap nothing else (milk, ghee, sugar are normally accepted) (not source-checked; families differ)

ekadashi.reason: Not found — carrot is a root vegetable and rules on roots differ by family; no source was checked this run

jain.reason: carrot is a root vegetable (Patch 05); the dish cannot be made Jain without replacing the carrot

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; a sweet, rich bowl that suits iftar in a small portion but is high in sugar (about 25 g added) and saturated fat for sehri

jain.reason: carrot is a root vegetable (Patch 05 rule) and the dish is defined by it; ghee and milk are fine, but the carrot cannot be swapped without making a different dish

vegan.reason: milk 150 ml and ghee 12 g are dairy; use thick coconut milk and coconut oil (see Vegan variant)

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat or egg

sattvik.reason: no onion or garlic in the recipe

glutenFree.reason: carrot, milk, sugar, ghee, cardamom, nuts; no wheat, rava, maida or hing

dairyFree.reason: milk and ghee; use the coconut milk and coconut oil version (see Dairy-free variant)

variants.reason: carrot is a root vegetable (Patch 05), and the dish is defined by it; a doodhi (bottle gourd) or other halwa is a different dish.
Main recipe already gluten-free (no wheat, rava, maida or hing).
